chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Hakeem, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'A non-Arab man and a weak woman are with the Bedouin cameleer. When he departs with them from 'Arafat, he passes with them just as he passed with them to Mina and does not encamp with them at Jam'. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Is it not that they prayed there, so it has sufficed them?' I said: 'And if they did not pray there?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'They mention Allah in it. So if they had mentioned Allah in it, it has sufficed them.'

key_terms.الضَّعِيفَةُ: The weak one, referring to someone physically unable to perform strenuous rituals
key_terms.الْأَعْجَمِيُّ: Non-Arab, often used in classical texts to denote someone unfamiliar with local customs or language
key_terms.جَمْعاً: Jam', the specific area in Muzdalifah where pilgrims collect pebbles and stay overnight
key_terms.ذَكَرُوا اللَّهَ: They mentioned Allah, referring to dhikr (remembrance/invocation)
key_terms.عَرَفَاتٍ: Arafat, the plain where the main standing of Hajj occurs
key_terms.مُنًى: Mina, the tent city near Mecca

ai.seo_question: What is the substitute for prayer at Muzdalifah for those who cannot pray there?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the concession (rukhsah) for non-Arabs and the weak accompanying Arab camel drivers who may not stop at Muzdalifah for the combined prayer (Salat al-Jam'). Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that the essential requirement is the remembrance of Allah (dhikr) at the site, which suffices even if the formal prayer is missed, highlighting the flexibility in Hajj rituals for those with genuine constraints. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on the spirit of worship over rigid formalism when circumstances dictate.
